headline: Summer at Tranquility
summary: Roosevelt is at Tranquility, the family's summer house at Oyster Bay; no other details are recorded.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Thrown in a jumping spill
summary: Roosevelt has been rowing himself into shape, including a trip to Lloyd's Neck. Trying his horse over fences, he takes a hard fall when it rolls on top of him. That evening he sails with Emlen, West and Alfred to Matinecock Point to meet Elliott's boat carrying the Haddons, Douglas Robinson and Percy King.

events.detail: Rows to Lloyd's Neck to build condition
Horse falls and rolls over him at a jump
Evening sail to Matinecock Point with his cousins

tr_quotes.text: at one fence we got a regular cropper, the horse rolling right over on me.

uncertain: 'Al' read as cousin Alfred Roosevelt; 'Little Jane T.' surname not given.

headline: Independence Day with the crowd
summary: Roosevelt spends the Fourth with his friends and cousins, sailing, playing lawn tennis and jumping horses.

events.detail: Sailing, lawn tennis and horse jumping with friends

tr_quotes.text: We all spent the day together

headline: A moonlight sail
summary: A morning ride with Emlen schooling the horses over jumps is followed by a row around Hog Island with West and lawn tennis with the group. At night about twenty people take a moonlight sail and come home to dance, sing and swap stories.

events.detail: Teaches horses to jump on a ride with Emlen
Rows around Hog Island with West
Moonlight sail and dancing with a large party

tr_quotes.text: I am leading the most delightful life a fellow well could.

headline: Communion Sunday
summary: On Communion Sunday Roosevelt reflects that the plain Presbyterian service always sets him thinking, something he admits he rarely does on serious matters.

events.detail: Takes part in a Presbyterian communion service

tr_quotes.text: I like our simple Presbyterian form for this service so much; it always makes me think - and I generally do not do very much thinking on serious subjects.

headline: Overnight with the Dodges
summary: Roosevelt goes to stay a night with the Dodge family, whose sons Earl and Cleve he admires. They drive past the family's old summer places at Mosholu and Riverdale, and he sees the two Oyne boys.

events.detail: Visits the Dodge family overnight
Drives to old family haunts at Mosholu and Riverdale

tr_quotes.text: I like and respect both Earl and Cleve very much.

uncertain: 'Cleve' is likely Cleveland H. Dodge; kept as written.

headline: His mother turns 44
summary: Roosevelt's mother, Mittie, celebrates her 44th birthday while the family summers at Oyster Bay.

events.detail: Mother's 44th birthday

headline: Sixteen miles around Lloyd's Neck
summary: Roosevelt rows sixteen miles around Lloyd's Neck and reports that he is tanned to the waist and in top shape. Afternoons, once Elliott is up from the city, the brothers play tennis, wrestle and swim, and he sleeps soundly every night.

events.detail: Rows sixteen miles around Lloyd's Neck
Tennis, wrestling and swimming with Elliott

tr_quotes.text: Naturally I am in magnificent health and spirits.

headline: Training the horse to harness
summary: Cousin Alfred spends the day, and they row around Centre Island, play tennis and ride. Roosevelt begins teaching his horse to pull in harness. In the evening he dances at West's, where Gerty, Tiny and Virginia Roosevelt are guests.

events.detail: Rows around Centre Island with Alfred
Starts training his horse to harness
Dances at West's house with visiting cousins

tr_quotes.text: I am now training my horse to go in harness.

headline: The carefree charm of Oyster Bay
summary: Emlen takes a holiday to spend with Roosevelt, and they row around Centre Island. He writes that the mix of active outdoor life and freedom from care is what he loves most about Oyster Bay.

events.detail: Rows around Centre Island with Emlen

tr_quotes.text: a delightful sense of ease and absence of care - that consititutes the chief charm of Oyster Bay to me.

headline: A day with Elliott
summary: Elliott takes a day off, and the brothers sail and play tennis together. Roosevelt is teaching his horse to trot, thinking of hitching it to a tilbury next winter.

events.detail: Sailing and lawn tennis with Elliott
Trains his horse to trot for a light carriage

tr_quotes.text: Am teaching my horse to trot, as I think of putting him in a tilbury next winter.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Rowing thirty miles across the Sound
summary: Roosevelt rows across Long Island Sound to Sheffield Island light and back, about thirty miles. With the tide and no wind, the outward leg takes under three hours; the return, into a stiff headwind, takes four and a half and ships plenty of water. Charades and dancing follow at the crowded house.

events.detail: Rows to Sheffield Island lighthouse and back
Evening of dancing and charades with houseguests

tr_quotes.text: Rowed across the sound to Sheffield Island light and back, a distance of 30 miles.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Setting out on the Meteor
summary: Roosevelt, Alfred and West set off for a week aboard the Meteor, an open 24-foot sloop, stocked with hardtack, canned meat and coffee. The breeze dies by evening and they anchor off the Saugatuck River, sleeping in sailors' hammocks slung in the cockpit.

events.detail: Begins a week's cruise aboard the Meteor
Drops anchor where the Saugatuck River meets the Sound

tr_quotes.text: This trip we have sailors hammocks , which we sling in the cock pit - great improvment to our former way of sleeping on the boards.

headline: Sheltering at the Thimble Islands
summary: The Meteor weighs anchor at 5:30 into light headwinds. Roosevelt notes terns, gulls, coots and a storm petrel. Becalmed in the afternoon, they anchor off the Thimble Islands, then run for shelter behind one when a southerly wind kicks up at night.

events.detail: Sails east along the Connecticut shore
Sees terns, gulls, coots and a stormy petrel
Anchors at the Thimble Islands and shelters from a night wind

tr_quotes.text: I saw a good many terns and gulls and a few coots - also a stormy petrel.

headline: A rough beat to New London
summary: Low on water, the crew sails on Sunday despite Roosevelt's misgivings. Beating into a strengthening northeaster and a heavy sea, they struggle off Bartlett's Reef to keep the boat upright, taking on much water, and reach New London at 4 p.m.

events.detail: Beats into a northeast gale and reaches New London

tr_quotes.text: I don't like sailing on Sunday but we are short of water + must reach New London.

headline: Dinner with the Chapins, revolvers at sea
summary: The sailors call at the Chapins' house for dinner, then turn back into a strong southwesterly and put into Saybrook at sunset. Sharks and porpoises along the way serve as revolver targets.

events.detail: Dines at the Chapin family's house
Sails west and anchors at Saybrook
Takes revolver shots at sharks and porpoises

tr_quotes.text: Saw a shark or two and a good many porpoises

headline: Fighting out of Saybrook
summary: Leaving at 5 a.m., the Meteor battles over the shoals and tide rips at Saybrook's harbor mouth in a strong wind and big sea. Rain falls all morning, the breeze dies at noon, and they anchor in the lee of Charles Island at 7:30.

events.detail: Crosses the Saybrook shoals and sails to Charles Island

tr_quotes.text: At 7.30 we came to anchor under the lee of Charles Island.

headline: Rowing home in a dead calm
summary: Light, shifting winds give way to a flat calm from nine to six, and the crew labors at the long oars, not reaching Oyster Bay until 11:15 that night. Roosevelt judges the cruise a great success and his cousins fine company.

events.detail: Returns to Oyster Bay, much of the way under oars

tr_quotes.text: Al and Doc are not only good friends but extremely pleasant companions.
The trip has been a great success.

uncertain: 'Doc' read as West Roosevelt, the third member of the crew.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Friends worth having
summary: Roosevelt describes his days of riding, rowing, sailing, swimming and shooting, with one of his four cousin-companions staying over most days. He wishes John Elliott were there too. Evenings mean reading, whist or dancing, and he often takes Miss Hale of Philadelphia, a guest of Aunt Lizzie's, out rowing.

events.detail: Daily round of outdoor sports
Rows with Miss Hale, a guest of Aunt Lizzie

tr_quotes.text: By Jove, those five are friends worth having.

headline: Against too much slaughter
summary: Roosevelt writes to fellow naturalist Henry Minot that he has collected little this summer because he disapproves of killing too many specimens.

events.detail: Letter to Henry Minot about collecting

letters.topic: Why he has collected few specimens this summer

tr_quotes.text: I have not done much collecting this summer for, as you know, I don't approve of too much slaughter.

uncertain: Henry Minot identified as Henry Davis Minot, TR's ornithologist friend.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Alice Lee turns 18
summary: While Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay, Alice Lee marks her 18th birthday at Chestnut Hill.

events.detail: Alice Lee's 18th birthday

headline: Racing Elliott around Lloyd's
summary: Elliott stays out from town and the brothers row fifteen miles around Lloyd's Neck, racing nearly all the way. Roosevelt sizes them up as evenly matched athletes: Elliott the better rower, sailor, swimmer and shotgun hand; he the better runner, wrestler, boxer and rifle shot.

events.detail: Fifteen-mile rowing race with Elliott around Lloyd's Neck

tr_quotes.text: As atheletes we are about equal; he rows best; I run best; he can beat me sailing or swimming; I can beat him wrestling or boxing. I am best with the rifle, he with the shotgun

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Twelve hours after woodcock
summary: Roosevelt hunts woodcock with young Pendleton Cruger from seven in the morning to seven at night through brutal cover in the heat, wading waist-deep in mud holes and swamps. Cruger shoots well; Roosevelt says he does not. They bag seven birds.

events.detail: Day-long woodcock hunt with Pendleton Cruger; seven birds

tr_quotes.text: He is a pretty good shot - I am not.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: A big woodcock bag near Locust Valley
summary: Hunting with Cruger again, Roosevelt works Fleet's swamp, Townsend's and the Beekman place, then a string of boggy spots near Locust Valley. For once, he notes, he shoots very well.

events.detail: Woodcock hunt through several swamps toward Locust Valley

tr_quotes.text: I really shot very well today - rather an unusual incident with me.

uncertain: The record's tally reads 40 woodcock, which doesn't match the roughly 15 birds described; it may be a misreading.

headline: Rowing and riding with Emily Swan
summary: Roosevelt counts Emily Swan among the prettiest and most charming young women in Oyster Bay, and has enjoyed several rows and rides with her.

events.detail: Rows and rides with Emily Swan

tr_quotes.text: I have had several very pleasant rows and rides with her.

headline: A birthday book for Edith
summary: For Edith Carow's 18th birthday, Roosevelt gives her a copy of the verse novel Lucile, signing it as her sincere friend.

events.detail: Gives Edith Carow a book of poetry for her 18th birthday

tr_quotes.text: To Edith K. Carow on her eighteenth birthday from her sincere friend Theodore Roosevelt.

uncertain: The record names the poem 'Lucille' by 'Gwen Meredith'; the work is Lucile by Owen Meredith.

headline: Snipe hunting by skiff
summary: Roosevelt and Cruger take a skiff after snipe, rowing the beaches, poling through shallow lagoons and twisting marsh creeks, sailing when the wind allows and carrying the boat over several portages. The fast ebb sweeps them out of Lloyd's Neck so they need only steer and shoot.

events.detail: Snipe hunt by skiff through marshes and lagoons

tr_quotes.text: We had to make several portages.

uncertain: The number of snipe in the day's tally is unclear in the record.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Rowing, tennis and walks with Mother
summary: Roosevelt rows nearly every day, plays tennis with whichever cousins stay over, walks with his mother and takes his sisters Bamie and Corinne rowing. He is also giving Emily Swan tennis lessons.

events.detail: Near-daily rows to Lloyd's Neck or around Centre Island
Walks with his mother; rows with Bamie and Corinne
Teaches Emily Swan lawn tennis

tr_quotes.text: I often take Motherling out walking, or Bysie or Pussie out rowing.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: A poor day for woodcock
summary: Roosevelt and Cruger hunt woodcock all day, but the molting birds are scattered and both shoot badly, so they come home with just three.

events.detail: Woodcock hunt with Cruger; three birds

tr_quotes.text: The birds were moulting, however, and were very much scattered

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Junior grades top the class in zoology
summary: Roosevelt's junior-year marks arrive: an average above 87 percent, his best yet, and first in the class in zoology and political economy. Afternoons bring tennis and a swim with Elliott, and the horse is getting used to harness.

events.detail: Receives junior-year marks, averaging over 87 percent
Lawn tennis and swimming with Elliott

tr_quotes.text: In Zoology and Political Economy I lead every body.

headline: A happy home
summary: Roosevelt notes the family's Sunday morning and evening prayers and wishes they were daily. He writes warmly of his mother, his sisters Bamie and Corinne, and Elliott, his best friend, who together make as happy a home as anyone could ask for.

events.detail: Sunday morning and evening family prayers

tr_quotes.text: Every Sunday we have morning, and evening prayers; I wish we could have them every day.
These three, and my best friend, old brother Nell, give me as happy a home as a man could possibly have.

headline: Weighing science or law
summary: On the eve of leaving for Maine, Roosevelt reflects on a fine, sunburned summer. He is thinking hard about life after college and expects either to pursue science or to read law as a path into public life.

events.detail: Prepares to leave for the Maine woods
Considers a scientific career or law study leading to public life

tr_quotes.text: am thinking pretty seriously as to what I shall do when I leave College; I shall probably either pursue a scientific course, or else study law, preparatory to going into public life.

uncertain: The quote's first word, 'I', is misprinted in the record, so the quote starts just after it.

headline: Dinner at the University Club
summary: In New York Roosevelt praises his guardians, Uncle Jim Roosevelt and Uncle Jimmie Gracie, as the best he could have. That evening Douglas Robinson joins him for dinner at the University Club, along with Haddon, Stratton, Sedgwick and Kingsford.

events.detail: Goes from Oyster Bay into New York
Meets with his guardians
Dinner at the University Club

tr_quotes.text: I wonder if there could be two better guardians than Uncle Jim Roosevelt and Uncle Jimmie Gracie! I can't imagine it.

uncertain: 'Uncle Jim Roosevelt' taken as James A. Roosevelt; 'Haddon' assumed Harold Haddon.

headline: Warm welcome at Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt travels to Boston and on to Chestnut Hill, where Dick Saltonstall greets him heartily. After dining with Mrs. Lee they drive to the Whitneys', where Bessie, Rose, Rosy Lee and Alice are staying, and plan a picnic for Ell Whitney's birthday.

events.detail: Travels to Boston and Chestnut Hill
Dines with Mrs. Lee, then visits the Whitneys

tr_quotes.text: dear old Dick gave me the most hearty and enthusiastic greeting.

headline: Picnic day at the Whitneys'
summary: Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive to the Whitneys' at nine and stay past midnight, sailing, walking, dancing and playing tennis. He is especially glad to see Rose and Alice again.

events.detail: Birthday outing at the Whitneys' with a large party

tr_quotes.text: The Whitneys are exceedingly hospitable and cordial.

headline: Turning down Alice to keep a promise
summary: Roosevelt visits Rose, Rosy Lee and Alice in town as they leave for the Slades', and they press him to come along. Alice is so lovely that refusing is hard, but he keeps his promise to meet Emlen and takes the night train for Mattawamkeag after dinner with Frank Lee at the Union Club. On the train he writes Bamie about his Boston stay.

events.detail: Sees Rose, Rosy Lee and Alice off to the Slades'
Dines with Frank Lee at the Union Club
Night train for Mattawamkeag, Maine
Letter to Bamie from the train

letters.topic: His Boston visit with Alice and why he left for Maine

tr_quotes.text: Alice was so bewitchingly pretty that it was frightfully hard to refuse.

headline: Back in the Maine woods
summary: Roosevelt reaches Mattawamkeag at 10 a.m. and drives to Island Falls with Dave Sewall. Emlen and Arthur Cutler are there, and he plans a short trip with them to Mount Katahdin.

events.detail: Reaches Mattawamkeag and drives to Island Falls
Plans a Katahdin trip with Emlen and Arthur Cutler

tr_quotes.text: I shall make a short trip with them to Katahdin.

uncertain: The record spells the name 'Seawall'.

headline: Packing for Katahdin
summary: Roosevelt spends the day getting ready, listing his kit: two changes of clothes, wool socks, a flannel shirt, duck trousers, a blanket and thick jacket, plus rifle and shotgun.

events.detail: Prepares gear for the Katahdin trip

tr_quotes.text: I have taken both rifle + shot gun.

headline: Paddling the lake with Emlen
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen paddle about 25 miles to their former campsite at the lake's lower end and back. No partridges turn up, but he picks up wood ducks along the channels and praises Emlen and Arthur as good-natured trail partners.

events.detail: Canoes about 25 miles round trip with Emlen
Shoots wood ducks

tr_quotes.text: Em + Arthur are capitel fellows for a trip of this kind -unselfish, good natured, and not minding a little fatigue + hardship.

uncertain: Lake not named; taken as Mattawamkeag Lake from the March trip.

headline: Starting for Katahdin with a 45-pound pack
summary: Roosevelt, Emlen, Arthur Cutler, Will Dow and Bill Sewall set out for Mount Katahdin, driving 23 miles and then backpacking about ten before camping. He carries roughly 45 pounds and loses a shoe in a stream crossing, luckily having moccasins tied to his pack.

events.detail: Sets out for Mount Katahdin by wagon and on foot
Loses a shoe fording a stream; switches to moccasins

tr_quotes.text: I carried about 45 lbs, including my gun + cartridges.

headline: Campfire at Katahdin Lake
summary: The party walks to the upper end of Katahdin Lake and makes camp. Roosevelt stalks and kills four ducks, adds two grouse, and they land some trout. By day the black flies are fierce, but evenings around the blazing fire feel like old times.

events.detail: Treks to the upper end of Katahdin Lake
Kills ducks and grouse; fishes for trout

tr_quotes.text: It is very pleasant + Like old times in the evenings, round the roaring logs of the camp fire.

headline: Lost after dark
summary: After a morning partridge hunt the group heads for Katahdin, catching about a hundred trout at Sandy Brook. Then they lose their way, push through terrible ground into the night, and camp beside a small water hole, soaked, worn out and hungry yet happy. Fresh bear and caribou tracks are everywhere.

events.detail: Morning partridge hunt
Lands roughly a hundred trout in Sandy Brook
Gets lost and camps by a water hole after dark

tr_quotes.text: wet, tired and hungry - but happy.

headline: Climbing Mount Katahdin
summary: Starting before dawn, Roosevelt climbs Mount Katahdin through hard terrain; Emlen and Arthur give out before the top, but he reaches the summit and its fine view. He finds he can bear fatigue nearly as well as the woodsmen. Back at Katahdin Lake by dark, in rain, with about 60 trout.

events.detail: Climbs to the summit of Mount Katahdin
Follows a blazed trail back to camp at Katahdin Lake

tr_quotes.text: I find I can endure fatigue + hardship pretty nearly as well as these lumbermen.

uncertain: The record says Emlen and Arthur stopped short; the two backwoodsmen are presumably Dow and Sewall.

headline: Scarce game around the lake
summary: Roosevelt circles half the lake in the morning without seeing anything, then walks down Sandy Brook in the afternoon and takes a black duck on Moose Pond. Small trout are plentiful, but game is sparse or out of reach.

events.detail: Hunts around Katahdin Lake and along Sandy Brook
Shoots a black duck on Moose Pond

tr_quotes.text: Trout of small size are very plentiful.

headline: A lazy Sunday in camp
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday around camp cleaning guns, mending clothes and bathing in the lake. The black flies torment his companions but hardly trouble him, and though game is scarce he is having a grand time.

events.detail: Camp chores and a swim in the lake

tr_quotes.text: You get pretty dirty in camp.
but I am enjoying myself exceedingly.

headline: Breaking camp for Island Falls
summary: Up before sunrise, Roosevelt hunts the bogs around a barrens pond and wounds a duck that escapes into the rushes. In the afternoon the party shoulders packs and heads for Island Falls, camping after crossing the Wassataquoik. He says he can now walk, wrestle and shoot with most of the lumbermen.

events.detail: Dawn duck hunt around the bogs
Breaks camp and hikes toward Island Falls, crossing the Wassataquoik

tr_quotes.text: Am in beautiful condition; + I find I can walk, wrestle + shoot with most of these lumbermen.

uncertain: The record spells the stream 'Wissaticock'.

headline: Katahdin trip ends at Island Falls
summary: The party hikes to the Penobscot's East Branch, fords it and rides on to Island Falls. Roosevelt calls the trip a delight and his companions excellent company.

events.detail: Fords the Penobscot's East Branch and returns to Island Falls

tr_quotes.text: I have enjoyed the trip exceedingly; the boys are most pleasant companions.

headline: Buckboard hunt comes up empty
summary: Roosevelt spends the afternoon riding around in a buckboard in search of partridges, without seeing a single bird.

events.detail: Unsuccessful partridge hunt by buckboard

tr_quotes.text: Spent the afternoon driving about in a buckboard looking for partridges; but saw none.

headline: Outfitting a canoe trip with Sewall
summary: Roosevelt prepares for a trip to the Munsungan waters, just he and Bill Sewall in a canoe. He packs tea, pork, hardtack and flour, a shelter tent, two blankets, spare underclothes and plenty of ammunition, and plans to wear only moccasins. He writes Bamie that moccasins served his feet well on Katahdin.

events.detail: Packs for a canoe trip with Sewall
Letter to Bamie about moccasins on the Katahdin climb

letters.topic: How moccasins protected his feet climbing Katahdin

tr_quotes.text: I shall go in a canoe alone with Seawall.
I shall only use moccasins.

uncertain: The record spells the Munsungan waters more than one way ('Munsingon', 'Munsingan').

headline: Forty-five miles to the Aroostook Oxbow
summary: Setting off before dawn by farm wagon, Roosevelt and Sewall cover 45 miles of thinly settled forest and some burned-over land to reach the Oxbow of the Aroostook by 6 p.m. They lodge in a bare-bones backwoods house. From the wagon he shoots a spruce grouse and a red-tailed hawk.

events.detail: Wagon journey to the Oxbow of the Aroostook River
Bags a spruce grouse and a red-tailed hawk while riding

tr_quotes.text: fare and sleeping accomodations being both primative to a degree.

headline: Poling up the Aroostook in a dugout
summary: In a dugout that handles rough going better than birchbark, the pair works some twenty miles upriver on the Aroostook, mostly poling. The country is wild and lovely, with no sign of people or game, though trout abound. They camp before dark to cook bread, trout and partridge.

events.detail: Poles a dugout some twenty miles upriver
Camps and cooks trout and partridge

tr_quotes.text: The scenery is very beautiful and wild; I saw no trace of man - but also no trace of game.

headline: Wading the Munsungan in the rain
summary: They push on despite the Sabbath, though Roosevelt neither shoots nor fishes. After poling to the Munsungan's mouth by lunchtime, they wade upstream hauling the boat, sometimes hip-deep, in heavy rain, and camp at dusk soaked and spent.

events.detail: Observes Sunday by not hunting or fishing
Drags the boat up the Munsungan Stream in rain

tr_quotes.text: I compromised by not shooting or fishing.

uncertain: The record spells the Munsungan waters more than one way ('Munsingon', 'Munsingan').

headline: Beaver dams, falls and a lovely time
summary: In steady rain they drag the heavy dugout through rapids, cut through beaver dams and logjams, unload it to climb past falls, then paddle across the lower Munsungan Lake and halfway up the middle one to camp. Roosevelt is cold, wet and hungry but still enjoying himself, though there is no sign of game.

events.detail: Hauls the dugout upstream and paddles into the Munsungan Lakes

tr_quotes.text: Tired out, + wet through, hungry + cold - but am having a lovely time.

uncertain: The record spells the Munsungan waters more than one way ('Munsingon', 'Munsingan').

headline: Turning back for lack of game
summary: Through more rain they paddle up the middle lake and slog over brutal terrain to the top of the upper lake. Roosevelt finds only old moose sign, a fresh bear track, a few grouse, loons and mergansers, so he decides to head back to Island Falls rather than stay as planned.

events.detail: Paddles and hikes to the upper Munsungan Lake
Notes moose and bear tracks, loons and fish ducks
Shoots three ruffed grouse

tr_quotes.text: although the work is very hard, I am enjoying the trip greatly.

uncertain: The record spells the Munsungan waters more than one way ('Munsingon', 'Munsingan').

headline: Running the rapids downstream
summary: Starting before sunrise, Roosevelt and Sewall paddle out of the lakes, run the falls, wade the quick water and then pole swiftly downstream, reaching Saturday's campsite by early afternoon. He treasures the evenings by the fire under their small tent.

events.detail: Descends from the Munsungan Lakes to the Aroostook

tr_quotes.text: I am very fond of the evenings round the camp fire, beneath the little tent.

uncertain: The record spells the Munsungan waters more than one way ('Munsingon', 'Munsingan').

headline: Living off the land
summary: They paddle down to the Oxbow, where Roosevelt shoots a wood duck, then walk about 15 miles, partly overland, to a crude farmhouse in the woods. Food is plain but there is good milk, and with a rabbit and a partridge taken on the way they supply their own meat.

events.detail: Paddles to the Oxbow and walks 15 miles to a backwoods house
Takes a wood duck, a rabbit and a ruffed grouse

tr_quotes.text: we have shot our own meat

headline: Twenty miles to a cranberry-bog pond
summary: Roosevelt walks over 20 miles round trip through the woods to a bog pond ringed with cranberries, shooting a duck there and picking up two grouse and a hawk along the way.

events.detail: Long walk to a bog pond; shoots a duck, two grouse and a hawk

tr_quotes.text: The walking was pretty good.

headline: Footsore return to Island Falls
summary: A 25-mile walk through the forest brings Roosevelt back to Island Falls, past waterfalls in deep ravines, with five grouse shot on the way. One moccasin is nearly worn through and his feet are sore.

events.detail: Walks about 25 miles back to Island Falls
Shoots five ruffed grouse

tr_quotes.text: Wore one of my moccasins almost out, which made me rather footsore.

headline: Admiring the Yankee backwoodsmen
summary: Roosevelt attends church, reads his Bible and spends the day shaving, bathing and readying for another expedition. He praises the backwoods meeting houses and the hunters, lumbermen and farmers of the region. To Bamie he writes that the Katahdin outing was luxury next to this second trip.

events.detail: Attends a backwoods church and reads his Bible
Prepares for a new expedition
Letter to Bamie about the hard Munsungan trip

letters.topic: Compares his rugged second trip with the Katahdin outing

tr_quotes.text: I don't know a better or more intelligent race of men than these shrewd, plucky, honest Yankees - all of them hunters, lumbermen or small farmers.
our trip to Katahdin was absolute luxury.

headline: Rained in
summary: Steady rain keeps Roosevelt from starting out.

events.detail: Delays departure because of rain

tr_quotes.text: Rained all day, so did not start.

headline: Rough road, rougher cabin
summary: Roosevelt and Bill Sewall set out by wagon behind an unruly horse over bad roads, stopping after about 30 miles at a very crude cabin.

events.detail: Thirty-mile wagon trip with Sewall to a backwoods cabin

tr_quotes.text: Started with Bill, in a rough wagon with a rougher horse; the roads were rougher still; and the cabin we are now staying in, after going about 30 miles, is roughest of all.

headline: A welcome at Littlefield's clearing
summary: Roosevelt walks about 25 miles through the woods to a backwoods homestead run by a settler named Littlefield, who looks after them well. He shoots spruce grouse in a spruce thicket and a tamarack swamp.

events.detail: Walks about 25 miles to Littlefield's clearing
Shoots two spruce grouse

tr_quotes.text: where we were very well treated.

headline: Tough as a pine knot
summary: Walking back to the horse, Roosevelt kills four grouse, then drives to Island Falls and shoots a pigeon from the wagon. Two weeks of foul weather have not dampened him; he feels superbly healthy.

events.detail: Walks back to the wagon and drives to Island Falls
Kills four grouse and a pigeon

tr_quotes.text: as tough as a pine knot.

headline: To the foot of Mattawamkeag Lake
summary: Roosevelt walks through the woods to the lower end of Mattawamkeag Lake, where he camps.

events.detail: Walks to the foot of Mattawamkeag Lake

tr_quotes.text: Walked down through the woods

headline: Seven grouse from one flock
summary: On a 20-mile walk Roosevelt takes two partridges on a hemlock ridge and then seven from a flock of eight in a river meadow. At rifle practice that afternoon he shoots well, though Dow and Sewall shoot better.

events.detail: Kills nine ruffed grouse on a 20-mile walk
Rifle practice with Dow and Sewall

tr_quotes.text: I shot very well, but not as well as Dow and Seawall.

headline: Luxury and hardship, both enjoyed
summary: Roosevelt paddles to Island Falls for the night and packs to leave. A porcupine that wanders into camp is chased off with a tin dipper. He marvels at the swings of his year between high living and hard toil, both of which he loves.

events.detail: Paddles to Island Falls and packs up
Drives a porcupine out of camp with a dipper

tr_quotes.text: What glorious fun I am having this year!
And my life has such absurd contrasts. At one time I live in the height of luxury; and then for a month will undergo really severe toil and hardship - and I enjoy both extremes almost equally.

headline: Down the Mattawamkeag by birchbark
summary: Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow start down the Mattawamkeag in a birch canoe, covering about ten miles below the lake. He and Dow circle through the woods to ambush a flock of mergansers, and he misses some long rifle shots at loons and cranes. He will hate to end the trip but is eager to get back to Harvard.

events.detail: Canoes down the Mattawamkeag River
Ambushes mergansers with Dow; misses long shots at loons and cranes

tr_quotes.text: I shall be very sorry to end this trip; and yet how I shall enjoy getting back to Harvard.

headline: Camp below Wytopitlock
summary: The canoe party paddles past Wytopitlock and camps. Dow shoots well at ducks and pigeons while Roosevelt misses most, but he redeems himself with rifle shots at hawks and owls. Muskrat and merganser both prove good eating.

events.detail: Paddles down past Wytopitlock and camps
Shoots poorly at birds but well at hawks and owls with the rifle

tr_quotes.text: both it + the fish ducks were very good eating!

uncertain: The record spells it 'Wytipitlock'.

headline: Leaving Maine strong as a bull
summary: Roosevelt paddles about 12 miles of still water to Kingman and takes the train to Boston, sorry to part from Sewall and Dow after a superb month. He feels immensely strong and almost fears his happiness is too great to last.

events.detail: Paddles to Kingman and boards the train for Boston

tr_quotes.text: Am feeling as strong as a bull.
By jove, it sometimes seems as if I were having too happy a time to have it last. I enjoy every moment I live, almost.

headline: Senior year begins with a stylish rig
summary: Back in Cambridge, Roosevelt is greeted by his friends with noisy delight. He boards his horse and a new dogcart at Pike's Stable and expects a fine winter.

events.detail: Returns to Harvard for senior year
Keeps his horse and dogcart at Pike's Stable

tr_quotes.text: I intend to have lovely fun this winter.

headline: Feeling at home at Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt drives Dick Saltonstall to Chestnut Hill, where the welcome is so warm he feels he has come home.

events.detail: Drives Dick Saltonstall to Chestnut Hill

tr_quotes.text: I felt as if I had come home.

headline: Tennis at Minot Weld's and gifts for the Saltonstalls
summary: Roosevelt drives Harry Chapin to a tennis party at Minot Weld's with Rose, Rosy Lee, Alice and others, then goes to the Saltonstalls' for Sunday, bringing a gun for Phil, toy soldiers for Cotty and pins for Rose and Mrs. Saltonstall. It is also Corinne's 18th birthday.

events.detail: Lawn tennis party at Minot Weld's
Arrives at the Saltonstalls' with gifts
Corinne turns 18

tr_quotes.text: My cart is the greatest success of the season.

uncertain: The record identifies 'Mamie' as Mrs. Saltonstall in its October 17 entry.

headline: Sunday with the Saltonstalls
summary: Roosevelt enjoys his Sunday at Chestnut Hill with the Saltonstalls and takes Rose for a walk in the afternoon.

events.detail: Stays with the Saltonstalls; walks with Rose

tr_quotes.text: I am having a lovely time.

headline: Italian and political economy
summary: Roosevelt begins logging his study hours: Italian prep and recitation in the morning, then political economy, six hours in all. He is thrilled with his horse and cart, and tells Bamie he came back from Maine tough as a pine knot.

events.detail: Studies Italian and political economy for six hours
Letter to Bamie about his health and new cart

letters.topic: His toughness after Maine and his new horse and cart

tr_quotes.text: I am perfectly delighted with the horse and cart
tough as a pine knot

headline: Zoology at the Museum, geology in the field
summary: Roosevelt puts in eight hours: zoology at the Museum through the morning, geology fieldwork in the afternoon and political economy at night. After dark he pays a call on the Lane sisters.

events.detail: Zoology at the Museum and geology fieldwork
Evening call on the Lane sisters

tr_quotes.text: 9-1 work at my zoology course in the Museum, 2-5 Field work in Geology.

headline: Naming his closest friends
summary: After six hours of Italian, political economy and a geology lecture, Roosevelt takes his cart out as he does most afternoons. He ranks Dick Saltonstall as his closest friend at Harvard, ahead of Harry Shaw, Minot Weld, Harry Chapin and John Tebbetts, and as dear to him as his Roosevelt cousins.

events.detail: Italian, political economy and a geology lecture
Afternoon drive in his cart

tr_quotes.text: Old Dick I place on a par with the Roosevelts.

headline: Moonlit drive from the Whitneys'
summary: After zoology and political economy, Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive his cart to the Whitneys' for the evening and return under a full moon.

events.detail: Zoology course and political economy study
Evening at the Whitneys' with Dick Saltonstall

tr_quotes.text: The drive home was delightful, there being a most beautiful full moon.

uncertain: Header line begins with a stray '8 1/2'.

headline: Dinner with new acquaintances
summary: Following his usual six hours of classes, Roosevelt dines at the Saltonstalls', where Rosy Lee, Mary Tuckerman and the delightful Harriet Lawrence are guests.

events.detail: Italian, political economy and geology
Dinner at the Saltonstalls'

tr_quotes.text: a most charming girl, Harriet Lawrence.

headline: Thirty-six hours a week
summary: Roosevelt tallies his schedule at about 36 hours of study a week. He takes Minot Weld on a long cart ride and ends the night with a boisterous party at the club.

events.detail: Zoology and geology review
Long drive with Minot Weld; late night at the club

tr_quotes.text: In all I work 36 hours a week - generally a little more.

uncertain: 'Minot' read as Minot Weld.

headline: Porcellian breakfasts resume
summary: The Porcellian's Sunday morning breakfasts start up again, and in the afternoon Roosevelt and Harry Chapin walk into Boston to call on the Hoopers.

events.detail: Sunday breakfast at the Porcellian
Calls on the Hooper family with Harry Chapin

tr_quotes.text: Recommenced our usual Sunday morning Porcellian breakfasts.

headline: At Harvard in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: At Harvard in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Training to run
summary: Roosevelt drives out every afternoon and finds his horse a quick trotter. He is also training as a runner, covering about a mile a day at roughly a 5:15 pace.

events.detail: Daily mile run in training
Afternoon drives in his cart

tr_quotes.text: Am training for running.

headline: A quick call, then the theater
summary: Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive to Chestnut Hill, but he cuts the visit short to make the theater with Harry Shaw.

events.detail: Brief call at Chestnut Hill with Dick Saltonstall
Theater with Harry Shaw

tr_quotes.text: only stayed a very short time

headline: Officer of half the clubs on campus
summary: Roosevelt complains of too many club duties: he keeps the Porcellian's library, serves as Pudding secretary, treasurer of the O.K., second in command at the Natural History Society, head of the A.D.G. club and an editor of the Advocate. Evenings go to whist, billiards and late suppers at the club.

events.detail: Lists his offices in college clubs and societies
Evenings of whist and billiards at the club

tr_quotes.text: I have my hands altogether too full of society work

headline: A rowdy roommate for the night
summary: After a big Porcellian supper, Dick Saltonstall and Jack Tebbetts come to the club, and a tipsy Dick sleeps in Roosevelt's room, to its considerable damage.

events.detail: Porcellian supper; Dick Saltonstall stays over

tr_quotes.text: Had a great Porc. Supper

headline: Nursing Dick, walking with Rosy and Rose
summary: With Dick feeling the effects of the night before, Roosevelt drives him to Chestnut Hill after a late club breakfast. He has tea at the Saltonstalls' and takes walks with Rosy Lee and then Rose.

events.detail: Drives a hungover Dick home to Chestnut Hill
Tea at the Saltonstalls'; walks with Rosy Lee and Rose

tr_quotes.text: Dick being decidedly under the weather from last nights spree

headline: Nineteenth in the class
summary: Roosevelt drives Jack Tebbetts to call on the Bacon sisters, pleased that his cart rides smooth as a cradle. He tells Bamie he ranks 19th in his class and sends Corinne an outline of his schedule.

events.detail: Calls on the Bacon sisters with Jack Tebbetts
Writes Bamie about his class rank
Writes Corinne about his schedule

tr_quotes.text: the cart rides as easily as a cradle.
I stand 19th in the class.

uncertain: 'Miss Bacons' taken as Nellie and Julia Bacon.

headline: A missing diary page
summary: The diary page for this day and the next was torn out. A later letter to his mother indicates that sometime in these two days Roosevelt dined at the Lees'.
uncertain: Diary page missing; the Lee dinner could fall on Oct 14 or 15.

headline: An evening at the Lees'
summary: Per a letter to his mother written five days later, Roosevelt dined at the Lees' around this time and had a wonderful evening with Rosy Lee, Alice and Rose.

events.detail: Dinner at the Lee home

tr_quotes.text: loveliest kind of an evening with Rosy, Alice and Rose

uncertain: Diary page missing; date of the dinner is either Oct 14 or 15.

headline: Visiting the Chinese professor
summary: Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall bring the Lane sisters along for a visit with the Chinese professor, an outing he found highly entertaining. His later letter home also refers to an evening at the opera with Alice.

events.detail: Call on the Chinese professor with the Lane sisters
Opera party with Alice

tr_quotes.text: had a most amusing time.

uncertain: The record does not give the date of the opera party.

headline: A birthday fan chain for Mrs. Saltonstall
summary: Roosevelt drives Minot Weld home, calls on George Minot, and stops briefly at the Saltonstalls' to wish Mrs. Saltonstall a happy birthday, giving her a small silver fan chain.

events.detail: Drives Minot Weld home; calls on George Minot
Birthday greeting and gift for Mrs. Saltonstall

tr_quotes.text: a small silver fan chain

headline: Tennis and a weekend with the Guilds
summary: Roosevelt plays tennis all morning with the Lane sisters, then drives Harry Guild to his family's home for Sunday. He likes the Guilds, who he notes are Harry Shaw's cousins.

events.detail: Morning tennis with the Lane sisters
Drives Harry Guild home for the weekend

tr_quotes.text: I like the Guilds very much.

headline: Church with the Bacons, tea at the Whitneys'
summary: Roosevelt walks the Bacon sisters home from church and drives to the Whitneys' for tea in the afternoon.

events.detail: Attends church
Walks the Bacon sisters home; tea at the Whitneys'

tr_quotes.text: Walked home from Church with the Miss Bacons

headline: A perfect morning drive
summary: Roosevelt drives home from the Guilds' on a glorious morning, the horse flying. That afternoon he and Van Rensselaer walk with Rose and Alice. He writes his mother a full account of his busy week and tells Henry Minot he can likely get to the White Mountains for a weekend in October.

events.detail: Morning drive back from the Guilds'
Walk with Rose and Alice alongside Van Rensselaer
Long letter to his mother about the week
Letter to Henry Minot about a White Mountains weekend

letters.topic: Detailed account of the week's activities
Plans a weekend trip to the White Mountains

tr_quotes.text: it was a divine morning and the little horse went like Sancho.
I do not have much spare time.
I think I can certainly get away to the White Mts. for a Saturday and a Sunday this October.

uncertain: Henry Minot taken as Henry Davis Minot.

headline: Edison's light bulb
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard; his own day goes unrecorded. Meanwhile, at Menlo Park, New Jersey, Thomas Edison achieves a working electric light bulb.

events.detail: Edison perfects the incandescent bulb at Menlo Park

headline: Thrown from the cart after the opera
summary: Roosevelt and Harry Shaw take the Saltonstall parents, Rose and Alice to the opera after dining at the Saltonstalls'. Leaving near midnight, the restless horse rears and falls, spilling both young men from the cart, but no one is hurt.

events.detail: Opera party for the Saltonstalls and Alice
Thrown from the cart when the horse rears and falls; unhurt

tr_quotes.text: Nothing was hurt however.

headline: Whist and late suppers
summary: Roosevelt takes Charley Morgan out for a drive. Most evenings he plays whist at the club or joins a theater party, and a habitual late supper keeps him up past bedtime.

events.detail: Drive with Charley Morgan
Evenings of whist at the club

tr_quotes.text: I find I don't get to bed very early.

headline: Night boat to New York
summary: Roosevelt drives Minot Weld home, noting that his horse goes well apart from rearing at the start and occasional shying. He then takes the overnight boat to New York.

events.detail: Drives Minot Weld home
Overnight boat to New York

tr_quotes.text: Took the night boat for New York.

headline: Home to the family
summary: In New York Roosevelt has breakfast and lunch at Aunt Lizzie's, then goes out to Oyster Bay, where Aunt Annie is staying. He is delighted to be with the family again.

events.detail: Breakfast and lunch at Aunt Lizzie's
Goes out to Oyster Bay

tr_quotes.text: It is perfectly lovely to see all the family again

headline: A classic Oyster Bay Sunday
summary: Roosevelt enjoys the familiar Oyster Bay Sunday routine: family prayers, a late breakfast, church, a long afternoon walk and an evening of hymn singing.

events.detail: Family prayers, church and evening hymns
Long afternoon walk

tr_quotes.text: Passed the usual dear old Oyster Bay Sunday

headline: Turning 21, thinking of Father
summary: Roosevelt celebrates his 21st birthday at Oyster Bay surrounded by his uncle James A. Roosevelt, Aunt Annie, Aunt Lizzie and cousins West, Emlen and Alfred; Emily Swan and other young women come for tea, charades and dancing. Amid the joy he thinks sadly of his late father and prays to live as he would have wished.

events.detail: 21st birthday gathering with relatives
Evening tea, dancing and charades

tr_quotes.text: My 21st birthday.

I have had so much happiness in my life so far that I feel, no matter what sorrows come, the joys will have overbalenced them, And yet on this day I can not help thinking with sadness about Father, my best and most loved and revered friend; may God help me to live as he would have wished.

uncertain: 'Doc' read as West Roosevelt and 'Uncle Jim' as James A. Roosevelt; quote keeps the diary's spelling 'overbalenced'.

headline: Tennis, walking and rowing
summary: Roosevelt fills the day at Oyster Bay with tennis, walks and rowing.

events.detail: Tennis, walking and rowing

tr_quotes.text: Spent the day playing tennis, walking and Towing.

uncertain: 'Towing' in the quote is a misprint for 'rowing'; the quote is left as printed.

headline: Bloodied in the catbrier
summary: Roosevelt spends twelve hours out with dog and gun. The morning brings rabbits and woodcock; in the afternoon he chases a wild covey of quail through catbrier so dense it soaks his shirt with blood, staying out past moonrise but shooting only two.

events.detail: All-day hunt for squirrels, rabbits, woodcock and quail
Arms and hands scratched bloody by catbrier

tr_quotes.text: a dense catbriar jungle which scratched my hands and arms till my shirt became soaked with blood

headline: Ducking on the Sound
summary: Roosevelt sails into Long Island Sound after ducks, but the few birds are wary and the wind is so strong he can barely handle the old fishing boat under a reefed sail. Back in the bay he finally downs a lone loon after many wasted shots.

events.detail: Duck hunting under sail on Long Island Sound
Shoots a stray loon in the bay

tr_quotes.text: so I did not get a shot.

headline: Quail hunting and a Halloween party
summary: Roosevelt drives with an old gunner named Ramson to a farmhouse eight miles away and spends six or seven hours in woods and stubble, whistling scattered quail back together. That evening he enjoys a Halloween party at the Swans', complete with the customary rituals and dancing.

events.detail: Quail, woodcock and rabbit hunt with the gunner Ramson
Halloween party at the Swan home

tr_quotes.text: The quail were plenty; but scattered easily and had to be whistled together.
